messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 27
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Journalist
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 64

He is a 27-year-old South Eastern Asian man who works as a journalist, and when he first begins telling the story, he stays careful with the details, as if naming them too directly might make them happen again. Before the violence, he describes himself as someone who moved quickly through the world: chasing deadlines, carrying a recorder in his pocket, always scanning for the next interview, the next angle, the next story worth telling. He liked the pressure of the job, the sense that he could be anywhere and make sense of it.

The relationship begins as something steady and unexpectedly comforting. He is drawn to how attentive his partner seems at first, how intensely they want to know him. The attention feels like care. He lets himself imagine a shared future. Over time, though, the care turns possessive. Small criticisms appear first—comments about what he wears, who he talks to, why he stays out late for work. He tries to adjust, telling himself that relationships require compromise, that his schedule is hard, that his partner is under stress. As a journalist, he is used to observing patterns before others do, but in his own life he misses the shape of what is building.

The abuse escalates gradually and then suddenly. He describes the first shove as something he almost excuses, a moment of heat and regret that he hopes will pass. It does not pass. Over time, there are hands on his arms hard enough to leave marks, objects thrown near him, walls struck inches from his face. Eventually, the assaults become direct. He remembers the shock of being hit by the person who also held his face while apologizing. The contradiction unsettles him more than the pain. He starts to feel as if he is living inside a split world: one in which he is still himself, still working, still answering emails and filing stories, and another in which he is waiting for the next explosion.

After one of the worst assaults, he notices how his body begins to keep the score for him. He startles at raised voices in restaurants, at a door closing too hard, at the sound of hurried footsteps behind him on the street. He sleeps lightly, with his phone beside him, waking at the slightest vibration. If he hears his partner’s key in the lock, his stomach tightens before he has time to think. He starts making small calculations about exits, how long it would take to leave, where he could go without being followed. At work, he remains composed on the surface, but colleagues notice he is distracted. He rereads the same paragraph several times. He misses a deadline once, then apologizes too quickly, embarrassed by how hard it is to concentrate.

He becomes increasingly isolated. He stops answering calls from friends because he does not want to explain the bruises, and because he has begun to fear that speaking about it will make it real in a way he cannot manage. He also feels shame, especially as a man, and especially as someone whose job depends on language and clarity. He has spent years asking difficult questions of other people, yet he cannot find the words to describe what is happening in his own home. He worries that if others knew, they would see him as weak, foolish, or complicit.

The relationship finally ends after an episode that leaves him physically shaken and fearful of what might come next. Leaving does not bring immediate relief. Instead, he finds that his mind keeps returning him to it in fragments: the look on his partner’s face, the sound of his own breathing, the sensation of bracing for impact. He avoids places that remind him of the relationship. He no longer likes unexpected touches, even from people he trusts. He is easily irritated, then guilty about the irritation. Some days he feels numb, moving through work and errands on automatic pilot. Other days he is flooded by memories that arrive without invitation and leave him disoriented for hours.

He is in a new relationship now, and although it matters to him, he finds himself measuring safety constantly. He watches for changes in tone, for a shift in posture, for any sign that affection might turn. He wants closeness and resents his own caution. He tells himself to stay present, but his body remains vigilant, always halfway elsewhere. Even as he continues reporting, meeting sources, and piecing together other people’s stories, he lives with the private knowledge that his own story has changed the way he moves through every room.
